# The disputes in full {#sec-appE}

Where a chapter stages a live scholarly disagreement, it keeps the finding and sends the argument
here. Nothing in this appendix is settled; that is the point of it. A reader who wants only the
state of play can stay in the chapters, and a reader who wants to know why the state of play is
unsettled will find the reasons below.

The appendix is organised by chapter, so that each chapter's live disagreements sit together and the
apparatus grows with the book rather than being retro-fitted to it.

# Chapter 1 — Deep structures

## Indus governance, three ways

The three positions run as a spectrum rather than a quarrel. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer argues for rulers
of a kind, reading the weight system as established by those rulers, plausibly for taxation --- but he
writes of the "so-called priest-king" himself and argues for several competing elite classes rather
than a single sovereign. Gregory Possehl denies a state in the archaic sense, with no king and no
royal apparatus, but affirms elites, ranks and a social pyramid, with authority perhaps sitting in
councils. Adam Green goes further than either, arguing for collective governance in which many
intersecting institutions rather than any ruling class coordinated labour and produced the public
goods: the water infrastructure, the large non-residential buildings, the planning itself.

The evidence Green leans on hardest is the distribution of the seals. More than a thousand were
recovered from the excavated areas of Mohenjo-daro alone, and on Franke-Vogt's analysis the great
majority came from ordinary households rather than large public structures. If seals recorded claims
on resources, the right to make such claims was spread very widely.

That inference is where the dispute actually sits. The step from where seals were found to how the
society was governed is an inference rather than a finding, and Possehl reads the same distribution as
a concentration in particular quarters rather than a random spread. Weights may have been used in
taxation, and at Harappa some were found by a neighbourhood gateway, though that has only been
reported preliminarily and does not hold across sites. What was taxed, and by whom, is unknown.

What the three agree on is enough to carry the economic argument without settling the dispute, and
that is why Chapter 1 does not try to settle it.

## Why the Indus cities emptied

Four readings are in play, and the chapter takes none of them as settled.

**Abrupt climate forcing.** Staubwasser and colleagues, and Gupta and colleagues, treat the 4.2 ka
event — a weakening of the monsoon around 2200 BCE — as the trigger. The difficulty is arithmetic: the
de-urbanisation is dated around 1900 BCE, three centuries later, and a mono-causal climate account has
to explain that lag away.

**Gradual hydrological change.** Giosan and colleagues emphasise rivers shifting and drying over
generations rather than a single sharp drought. This fits the palaeoclimate record better, which shows
no drought of the right timing and depth to topple a civilisation.

**Internal, ideological failure.** Gregory Possehl rejects environmental causation outright and
reaches for a failure of whatever held the civilisation together. His is an ideological explanation,
not a meteorological one.

**Flooding routed through politics.** Jonathan Mark Kenoyer keeps the water in the story but makes the
causal link political: the rivers moved, the disruption was real, and what broke was the legitimacy of
the people who had claimed to manage such things.

Two observations cut across all four. Both standard authorities attribute the drying of the Sarasvati
or Ghaggar-Hakra system to **tectonic change rather than monsoon failure**, which detaches the
most-cited piece of hydrological evidence from the climate story altogether. And on every reading,
"de-urbanisation" fits the evidence better than "collapse": the cities were given up, the population
shifted east toward the Ganges, and the people did not disappear.

^[**Sources:** Possehl, *The Indus Civilization* (2002), for the rejection of environmental causation
and the ideological reading; Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (1998), for
flooding mediated by a crisis of legitimacy, and both for the tectonic account of the Sarasvati;
Staubwasser et al. and Gupta et al. for abrupt forcing; Giosan et al. for gradual hydrological change.]

## Redistribution versus market at Uruk

Polanyi placed a redistributive pattern at the heart of the early Near East, and Uruk's state textile
workshops --- credited with as many as 9,000 women --- are the exhibit usually offered for it. Three
things complicate that.

**The chronology.** The archives documenting administered redistribution most fully are Ur III, around
2100 BCE, more than a millennium after Uruk. Emberling treats the great collection-and-redistribution
centres as an innovation of that empire rather than a feature of the first cities --- and Scott, the
source of the 9,000 figure, writes in the same passage that reading such evidence back to the Uruk
period "is highly questionable".

**The strongest version has been walked back.** The "temple-city" model, built on the archive of the
temple of Ba'u at Lagash, held that temples owned essentially everything. Continued study of that same
archive showed it had dramatically overstated how much land one temple held, and the Ba'u estate turns
out to have been supervised by the queens of Lagash rather than by a priesthood standing apart from
the palace.

**Emberling is more deflationary still:** markets, walls and temples cannot be used to explain why
cities arose, because none of them developed fully until later.

What survives into the chapter is the position it takes: redistribution and market dealing coexisted,
and the balance between them is contested rather than settled. The Uluburun cargo, a thousand years
later, shows both running in the same hold.

## The Phoenician metals question

The commercial thesis, argued at length by Susan Frankenstein and developed by Maria Eugenia Aubet,
holds that the western settlements were commercial factories and that the whole diaspora was a
response to Assyrian pressure on Tyre. The mining frontiers do open when the model predicts, in
south-western Spain and at Laurion in the Aegean.

The case against is archaeological, and it is not that the metals trade did not happen but that it
does not explain the settlements. The excavated colonies look like farms. They were agricultural towns
from their foundation --- wine and salted fish at Huelva by the eighth century, Gadir buying farmland
across the bay around 800 BCE --- and at ninth- and eighth-century Huelva, of some eight thousand
potsherds, 99.9 per cent are local or Phoenician and fewer than fifty are Greek. Nathan Pilkington
puts the negative sharply: the implication that Iberian metals were destined for Near Eastern markets
cannot, he argues, be corroborated from the archaeological record. The Phoenicians never permanently
settled the Atlantic tin coasts and abandoned the stations they did place there, and a direct run from
Tyre to Gadir was some four and a half thousand kilometres and a month's sailing, which allows one
voyage a season.

Where the field has moved is easy to overstate in either direction. The older scholarship explained
the colonies *exclusively* by trade in metals. The newer work, with specialised settlements, survey,
archaeobotany and archaeometallurgy, has opened the explanation to territorial, productive and social
motives alongside the commercial one. That is a broadening, not a refutation.

**What would settle it:** provenance work tying the silver in Levantine hoards to Iberian ores. This
book has not found that evidence either way.

^[**Sources:** on the Indus, Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (1998);
Possehl, *The Indus Civilization* (2002); Green, "Killing the priest-king" (2021) and his 2022 paper on
collective action; Franke-Vogt on the seal distribution. On the Phoenician question, Lopez-Ruiz and
Doak (eds), *The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean* (2019), and Pilkington,
*The Carthaginian Empire*, p. 61.]
